[Textbook misprint: the question as printed reads "vander Waals focres". Two defects in one phrase — the name is set as a single word where it is "van der Waals", and "focres" is a transposition of "forces". Transcribed as printed; neither affects the answer, which is physical adsorption (physisorption).]

Physical adsorption, also called **physisorption** — the adsorption in which the gas molecules are held at the surface of the solid only by weak van der Waals (London dispersion) forces.
Chemical adsorption, also called **chemisorption** — the adsorption in which the gas molecules are held on the surface by chemical bonds (covalent or ionic), so a surface compound is formed.

The Freundlich adsorption isotherm for the adsorption of a gas on a solid is

\(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,P^{1/n} \qquad (n > 1)\)

where \(x\) is the mass of gas adsorbed, \(m\) is the mass of the adsorbent, \(P\) is the equilibrium pressure, and \(k\) and \(n\) are constants that depend on the nature of the adsorbate, the adsorbent and the temperature. For adsorption from a solution the pressure is replaced by the equilibrium concentration \(C\), giving \(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,C^{1/n}\).

**a. Inhibition** — Inhibitors are substances that decrease the rate of a chemical reaction. Inhibition is therefore the retarding of a reaction by adding such a substance. For example, adding 2% ethanol to chloroform suppresses its air oxidation to carbonyl chloride, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\); ethanol acts as the inhibitor. Similarly, the decomposition of \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) is inhibited by a dilute acid or by glycerol.

**b. Electrophoresis** — The movement of colloidal particles under an applied electric potential is called electrophoresis. Positively charged particles move towards the cathode and negatively charged particles migrate to the anode, where they are deposited.

**c. Catalysis** — A catalyst is a substance which, when added to a reacting system, increases the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change. The phenomenon of altering the rate of a reaction by such a substance is called catalysis. It is of two types, homogeneous catalysis (reactants and catalyst in the same phase) and heterogeneous catalysis (reactants and catalyst in different phases).

**Adsorption** — Because the molecules or ions at the surface of a solid or a liquid have unbalanced (unsaturated) forces, the surface tends to attract gases or dissolved substances that come in close contact with it, so that the substance accumulates on the surface. This accumulation of a substance at the surface of a solid or a liquid is called adsorption. The substance on whose surface it happens is the **adsorbent**; the substance that gets held there is the **adsorbate**. Adsorption is a surface phenomenon — the adsorbate does not penetrate into the bulk.

**Why chalk writing stays readable on a blackboard** — When chalk is rubbed on the board, fine chalk particles are adsorbed on the surface of the board and are held there by the unbalanced surface forces. The board's surface is rough, and the chapter notes that rough surfaces and finely divided substances are good adsorbents because they offer a large surface area for a given mass, so a large quantity of chalk powder is retained on the board. The white chalk layer sticking on the dark surface is what the students see and read. Because the chalk is only held at the surface and not bonded into the bulk, it can be wiped off easily — that is, the adsorbed chalk is removed by desorption.

Characteristics of adsorption:

1. It is a **surface phenomenon** — the adsorbed matter is concentrated only at the surface and does not penetrate through the surface into the bulk of the adsorbent.
2. The **concentration of the adsorbate is high only at the surface** of the adsorbent, not uniform throughout.
3. It arises from the **unbalanced (unsaturated) forces** at the surface — London dispersion or van der Waals forces — which are short range and additive; the tendency to lower the surface energy is what causes adsorption.
4. It is an **exothermic process**, accompanied by the evolution of heat known as the heat of adsorption.
5. It **depends on temperature**. Being exothermic, it is favoured at low temperature; the amount of gas adsorbed is inversely proportional to temperature.
6. It **depends on pressure**. At any temperature the extent of adsorption increases with pressure, and at high pressure it becomes independent of pressure once the surface is almost fully covered.
7. It **depends on the surface area** of the adsorbent — finely divided substances, rough surfaces and porous solids are good adsorbents.
8. It is **reversible** in the case of physisorption; the adsorbed substance can be removed from the surface, a process called desorption.

| Lyophilic sols | Lyophobic sols |
|---|---|
| The particles of the dispersed phase have a great affinity for the dispersion medium. | The particles of the dispersed phase have no affinity for the dispersion medium. |
| Formed easily by direct mixing. | Formed only by special methods. |
| Reversible — if evaporated and the medium added again, the sol re-forms. | Irreversible — once coagulated they have little or no tendency to revert to the colloidal state. |
| The particles are not easily visible even under an ultramicroscope. | The particles are easily detected under an ultramicroscope. |
| These are self-stabilized. | These are unstable and hence require traces of stabilizers. |
| Addition of a **large** amount of electrolyte causes precipitation / coagulation. | Addition of a **small** amount of electrolyte causes precipitation / coagulation. |
| Viscosity of the dispersed phase is much higher than that of the dispersion medium. | Viscosity of the dispersed phase is nearly the same as that of the dispersion medium. |
| Surface tension of the dispersed phase is lower than that of the dispersion medium. | Surface tension of the dispersed phase is nearly the same as that of the dispersion medium. |
| Examples: starch, gum, gelatin sols. | Examples: sols of Ag and Au, hydroxides such as \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}\), metal sulfides. |

| Colloidal dispersion | Dispersed phase | Dispersion medium | Type of colloid |
|---|---|---|---|
| a. Milk | Liquid (fat) | Liquid (water) | Emulsion (oil in water) |
| b. Blood | Solid (plasma proteins and antibodies) | Liquid (water) | Sol |
| c. Printing ink | Solid (pigment / carbon particles) | Liquid | Sol |
| d. Fog | Liquid (water droplets) | Gas (air) | Aerosol |

The chapter states that milk consists of particles of fat dispersed in water, that blood is a colloidal dispersion of plasma proteins and antibodies in water, and that fog is formed of fine water droplets floating in air; Table 11.4 places a solid dispersed in a liquid (printing ink) among the sols and a liquid dispersed in a gas among the aerosols.

**a. Tyndall effect** — When light passes through a true solution its path cannot be detected, but when light passes through a colloidal dispersion the particles scatter some of it in all directions, so the path of the light becomes visible to an observer standing at right angles to it. This scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes the path of light visible through the dispersion, is called the Tyndall effect, and the bright cone of light is called the Tyndall cone. It is observed only when (i) the diameter of the dispersed particles is not much smaller than the wavelength of the light used and (ii) the refractive indices of the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium differ largely. It is used to determine the number and size of particles in a colloidal system and to distinguish a colloidal dispersion from a true solution.

**b. Brownian motion** — The colloidal particles undergo a ceaseless random zig-zag motion in all directions in the fluid; this motion of the dispersed-phase particles is called Brownian motion. It was observed by the British botanist Robert Brown in pollen grains under a microscope and explained by Albert Einstein in 1905. It is caused by the constant collisions of the dispersed-phase particles with the fast-moving molecules of the dispersion medium; the particles acquire kinetic energy from these molecules, and this brings forth the zig-zag motion.

**c. Types of emulsion** — An emulsion is a colloidal system in which one liquid is dispersed in another immiscible liquid. There are two types. In an **oil-in-water (o/w)** emulsion the dispersed phase is oil and the dispersion medium is water; examples are milk, vanishing cream and paint. In a **water-in-oil (w/o)** emulsion the dispersed phase is water and the dispersion medium is oil; examples are cod-liver oil, butter and cream.

**d. Hardy–Schulze rule** — Generally, the greater the valence of the flocculating ion added, the greater is its power to cause precipitation. For the coagulation of a negative sol the flocculating power follows the order \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}} > \mathrm{Ba^{2+}} > \mathrm{Na^{+}}\), and for the coagulation of a positive sol \(\mathrm{[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-}} > \mathrm{PO_4^{3-}} > \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} > \mathrm{Cl^{-}}\).

**Electrophoresis** — Colloidal particles carry an electric charge, and the charge is of the same sign on all the particles of a given sol. The movement of colloidal particles under an applied electric potential is called electrophoresis.

**Set-up (see the diagram)** — A U-tube is fitted with a reservoir and a stop cock, and the colloidal solution is taken in it. Two platinum electrodes, an anode and a cathode, are dipped into the sol. When an electric potential is applied across the two electrodes, the colloidal particles migrate towards one or the other electrode: positively charged particles move towards the cathode and negatively charged particles move towards the anode, and they get deposited on the respective electrode.

**Applications**
1. From the direction in which the colloidal particles move in the electric field, it is possible to know the sign of the charge on the particles.
2. It is used to measure the rate of migration of the sol particles.
3. A mixture of colloidal particles can be separated by electrophoresis, because different colloidal particles in a mixture migrate at different rates.

Adsorption is a surface phenomenon — the adsorbate accumulates only on the surface of the adsorbent and does not enter its bulk. Hence the extent of adsorption increases with an increase in the surface area of the adsorbent.

When a substance is finely divided, the same mass is broken up into a very large number of small particles, and the total exposed surface area for that given mass becomes much larger than that of one lump of the same mass. A finely divided substance therefore offers many more surface sites with unbalanced forces at which adsorbate particles can be held, and so it adsorbs an appreciably greater amount. This is why finely divided substances, rough surfaces and porous solids such as charcoal and silica gel are good adsorbents.

The relationship between the amount of a substance adsorbed per unit mass of the adsorbent and the equilibrium pressure (in the case of a gas) or the equilibrium concentration (in the case of a solution), at a given constant temperature, is called an adsorption isotherm. Various adsorption isotherms are known; the Freundlich adsorption isotherm \(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,P^{1/n}\) is one of them.

Raw sugar is coloured because of coloured impurities dissolved in the solution; the sugar itself is colourless. Animal charcoal is a porous, finely divided solid, and the chapter notes that charcoal is an effective adsorbent because of its porous nature, which gives it a very large surface area per unit mass.

When the aqueous solution of raw sugar is passed over beds of animal charcoal, the molecules of the coloured impurity are adsorbed on the large surface of the charcoal and are retained there, while the sugar and the water pass through. The solution that comes out is therefore colourless. This is the same behaviour as the chapter's own example of the removal of colouring matter: when charcoal is added to a solution of the organic dye methylene blue and shaken, the solution becomes colourless because the dye molecules accumulate on the surface of the charcoal.

The colloidal particles scatter the light in all directions, so the path of the beam through the sol becomes visible to an observer standing at right angles to the beam, and a bright cone of light — the Tyndall cone — is seen. This phenomenon is the **Tyndall effect**. It is seen only if the diameter of the dispersed particles is not much smaller than the wavelength of the light used and if the refractive indices of the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium differ largely. A true solution, by contrast, shows no such visible path, so this observation distinguishes a colloidal dispersion from a true solution.

All solids adsorb gases to some extent, and the extent of adsorption depends on the following factors:

1. **Nature of the adsorbate (gas)** — gases with a high critical temperature liquefy easily and are readily adsorbed.
2. **Nature of the adsorbent** — substances that provide a large surface area for a given mass, such as silica gel and charcoal, are effective adsorbents because of their porous nature.
3. **Surface area of the adsorbent** — the extent of adsorption increases with an increase in surface area, so finely divided substances, rough surfaces and colloidal substances are good adsorbents.
4. **Temperature** — adsorption is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle it is favoured at low temperature; the amount of gas adsorbed is inversely proportional to temperature.
5. **Pressure of the gas** — at any temperature the extent of adsorption increases with pressure, and at high pressure it becomes independent of pressure because the surface is then almost fully covered.

Four uses of adsorption:

1. **Heterogeneous catalysis** — solid catalysts adsorb the reactants and are used in many industrial processes; for example iron in the manufacture of ammonia, platinum in the manufacture of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) by the contact process, and finely divided nickel in the hydrogenation of oils.
2. **Gas masks** — a gas mask contains activated charcoal or a mixture of adsorbents and is used for breathing in coal mines, so that the poisonous gases are adsorbed and are not inhaled.
3. **Control of humidity** — silica and alumina gels are good adsorbents of moisture and are used to keep the surroundings dry.
4. **Production of high vacuum** — a vessel evacuated by a vacuum pump is connected to another vessel containing coconut charcoal cooled by liquid air; the charcoal adsorbs the remaining traces of air and moisture, and a high vacuum is attained.

(Other uses given in the chapter are adsorption indicators for the end point of precipitation titrations, separation of inert gases on coconut charcoal, the froth floatation process for concentrating a sulfide ore, and chromatographic analysis.)

**Bredig's arc method (electrical disintegration)** is a method for preparing colloidal sols of metals such as gold, silver and platinum. It involves both vaporization and condensation.

Two electrodes of the metal are immersed in the dispersion medium (water kept cooled in ice), and an electric arc is struck between them. The intense heat produced by the arc vaporizes the metal of the electrodes, and the metal vapour is at once cooled by the surrounding medium, so that it condenses to form particles of colloidal size. The result is a colloidal sol of the metal in the dispersion medium.

**Emulsion** — A colloidal system in which one liquid is dispersed in another immiscible liquid is called an emulsion. It is a liquid–liquid colloidal system in which the two liquids are completely or partially immiscible.

**Types**
1. **Emulsion of oil in water (o/w type)** — the dispersed phase is oil and the dispersion medium is water. Examples: milk (particles of fat dispersed in water), vanishing cream, paint.
2. **Emulsion of water in oil (w/o type)** — the dispersed phase is water and the dispersion medium is oil. Examples: cod-liver oil (particles of water dispersed in oil), butter, cream.

**Properties of emulsions** — an emulsion can be diluted with any amount of the dispersion medium, whereas the dispersed liquid when added forms a separate layer; the droplets are often negatively charged and can be precipitated by electrolytes; emulsions show Brownian movement and the Tyndall effect; and the two liquids can be separated by heating, freezing or centrifuging.

[Textbook note (not an error): the exercise asks this same question twice. It appears here as item 4 A, "A finely divided substance is more effective as adsorbent", and again as item 3 H, "Explain why finely divided substance is more effective as adsorbent?". Both are answered on the same ground — adsorption is a surface phenomenon, so a larger surface area for a given mass means greater adsorption.]

Adsorption takes place on the surface of the adsorbent, and the extent of adsorption increases with an increase in the surface area of the adsorbent.

On subdividing a solid, the same mass is distributed over a very large number of small particles, and the total surface exposed for that given mass increases greatly. A finely divided substance therefore presents many more surface sites carrying unbalanced forces at which the adsorbate can accumulate, and adsorbs a much larger amount than the same mass in one piece. This is the reason why finely divided substances, rough surfaces and porous solids such as charcoal and silica gel are used as adsorbents, and why finely divided metals such as platinum, palladium, copper and nickel adsorb gases like hydrogen and oxygen readily.

Freundlich proposed an empirical equation for the adsorption of a gas on a solid:

\(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,P^{1/n} \qquad (n > 1) \qquad \ldots (11.1)\)

where \(x\) is the mass of gas adsorbed, \(m\) is the mass of the adsorbent at pressure \(P\), so that \(x/m\) is the mass of gas adsorbed per unit mass of adsorbent, \(P\) is the equilibrium pressure, and \(k\) and \(n\) are constants depending on the nature of the adsorbate, the adsorbent and the temperature. For adsorption from a solution, \(P\) is replaced by the concentration \(C\):

\(\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,C^{1/n} \qquad \ldots (11.2)\)

Taking logarithms,

\(\log \dfrac{x}{m} = \log k + \dfrac{1}{n}\log C \qquad \ldots (11.3)\)

**Graph** — Plotting \(\log (x/m)\) against \(\log C\) (or \(\log P\)) gives a straight line. Its **slope is \(1/n\)** and its **intercept on the y-axis is \(\log k\)**, so both constants can be obtained from the plot (see the diagram).

**Discussion** — The factor \(1/n\) ranges from 0 to 1, and Eq. (11.3) holds good only over a limited range of pressures. When \(1/n \to 0\), \(x/m \to\) constant, that is the adsorption becomes independent of pressure. When \(1/n = 1\), \(x/m = kP\), that is \(x/m \propto P\) and the adsorption varies directly with pressure. A direct plot of \(x/m\) against \(P\) rises steeply at first and then tends to saturate at high pressure, because the surface of the adsorbent is then almost fully covered.

[Textbook misprint: section 11.2.3 of the chapter, which is the passage a student would turn to for the examples this question asks for, is headed "Examples of Absorption" but is mostly about ADSORPTION. It opens with one genuine absorption example (cotton dipped in water), then continues "Some more examples of adsorption :" and lists three adsorption examples — gases on finely divided metals, gases on activated charcoal, and the removal of an organic dye by charcoal. Those three are examples of adsorption, not of absorption, so the heading does not describe the section. The distinction itself is set out correctly in Table 11.1.]

| Adsorption | Absorption |
|---|---|
| Adsorbed matter is concentrated only at the surface and does not penetrate through the surface to the bulk of the adsorbent. It is a **surface phenomenon**. | Absorbed matter is uniformly distributed inside as well as on the surface of the bulk of the substance. It is a **bulk phenomenon**. |
| The concentration of the adsorbate is high only at the surface of the adsorbent. | The concentration of the absorbate is uniform throughout the bulk of the absorbent. |
| It is dependent on temperature and pressure. | It is independent of temperature and pressure. |
| It is accompanied by the evolution of heat, known as the heat of adsorption. | It is not accompanied by the evolution or absorption of heat. |
| It depends on the surface area. | It is independent of the surface area. |

**Examples** — Adsorption: a gas or a liquid such as acetic acid is adsorbed by activated charcoal. Absorption: water is absorbed by cotton (and ink by blotting paper).

(When adsorption and absorption occur simultaneously, as when a chalk is dipped in ink, the process is called sorption.)

| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| The forces operating are weak van der Waals forces. | The forces operating are chemical in nature (covalent or ionic bonds). |
| Not specific in nature — all gases adsorb on all solids. | Highly specific; occurs only when chemical bond formation is possible between adsorbent and adsorbate. |
| The heat of adsorption is low, in the range \(20\)–\(40\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). | The heat of adsorption is higher, in the range \(40\)–\(200\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). |
| Occurs at low temperature and decreases with an increase of temperature. | Favoured at high temperature; the extent is lowered at very high temperature because the bonds break. |
| Reversible. | Irreversible. |
| The adsorbed layer may be multimolecular under high pressure. | Forms a monomolecular layer of adsorbed particles. |

**Examples** — Physisorption: at low temperature \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas is physically adsorbed on iron (all gases adsorb on charcoal in the same way). Chemisorption: \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas chemically adsorbed on iron at high temperature forms a layer of iron nitride, which desorbs only at very high temperature (other examples are oxygen on tungsten and hydrogen on nickel).

Consider the surface of a liquid or a solid. The molecular forces at the surface of a liquid are unbalanced, or in an unsaturated state; in solids the ions or molecules at the surface of a crystal do not have their forces satisfied by close contact with other particles, because there are no neighbouring particles above them. Because of this unsaturation, solid and liquid surfaces tend to attract gases or dissolved substances with which they come in close contact, and the substance accumulates **on the surface**.

The particles in the interior (bulk) of the solid or liquid are surrounded on all sides and their forces are balanced, so they have no such tendency to attract and hold other particles. Hence the accumulation of the adsorbate is confined to the surface: the adsorbed matter is concentrated only at the surface and does not penetrate through the surface into the bulk of the adsorbent, and its concentration is high only at the surface. This is exactly what distinguishes adsorption from absorption, in which the absorbed matter is distributed uniformly throughout the bulk.

Two consequences confirm it. First, the extent of adsorption depends on the surface area of the adsorbent, so finely divided and porous substances that expose a large surface adsorb far more for the same mass. Second, the driving force is the tendency of the surface to lower its free energy (surface tension), which is a property of the surface alone. Adsorption is therefore a surface phenomenon.

**Nature of the adsorbate (gas)** — The amount of a gas adsorbed by a given solid depends on the nature of the gas. Gases having a high critical temperature liquefy easily and can readily be adsorbed. Thus gases such as \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_3}\), which are easily liquefiable, are adsorbed to a much larger extent than \(\mathrm{N_2}\), \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\), which are difficult to liquefy. The chapter's data show the trend clearly:

| Gas | Critical temperature / K | Volume adsorbed / \(\mathrm{cm^3}\) |
|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{N_2}\) | 126 | 08 |
| \(\mathrm{HCl}\) | 324 | 72 |
| \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) | 406 | 181 |
| \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) | 417 | 235 |
| \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) | 430 | 380 |

The volume adsorbed rises steadily as the critical temperature rises.

**Nature of the adsorbent** — Substances which provide a large surface area for a given mass are effective adsorbents and adsorb appreciable volumes of gases. Silica gel and charcoal are effective adsorbents because of their porous nature.

Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, so it can occur only where surface is available. Hence the extent of adsorption increases with an increase in the surface area of the adsorbent. Finely divided substances, rough surfaces and colloidal substances are good adsorbents because they provide a larger surface area for a given mass, and therefore a larger number of sites at which the gas can accumulate.

**1. Gas masks** — A gas mask is a device consisting of activated charcoal or a mixture of adsorbents. It is used for breathing in coal mines: the poisonous gases present in the air are adsorbed on the large surface of the activated charcoal as the air passes through the mask, so that they are not inhaled and only purified air reaches the wearer.

**2. Adsorption indicators** — Adsorption is used to detect the end point of precipitation titrations, using dyes such as eosin and fluorescein as indicators. For example, a solution of sodium chloride containing a small amount of fluorescein is titrated against silver nitrate solution:

\(\mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{AgNO_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{AgCl}\downarrow + \mathrm{NaNO_3}\)

AgCl separates as a white precipitate. Once the chloride ions are used up, the fluorescein is adsorbed on the white silver chloride precipitate and a red colour develops, so a colour change from pale yellow to reddish pink marks the end point.

(Other applications given in the chapter are heterogeneous catalysis, control of humidity by silica and alumina gels, production of a high vacuum, separation of inert gases, the froth floatation process and chromatographic analysis.)

Soap is an **associated colloid**. Substances of this kind behave as normal electrolytes at low concentration and associate at higher concentration to form a colloidal solution; the associated particles are called **micelles**.

A soap molecule has two very different ends: a long hydrophobic hydrocarbon chain, called the **tail**, attached to a hydrophilic ionic group (the carboxylate group), called the **head**. When soap is dissolved in water in sufficient concentration, these two ends cannot both be satisfied by the medium at once. The molecules therefore arrange themselves into spherical particles in which the **hydrophobic tails point inwards, towards the centre of the sphere**, away from the water, while the **hydrophilic ionic heads lie on the surface of the sphere**, in contact with the water. Such a spherical aggregate is a micelle.

Because the outside of each micelle is ionic and is therefore attracted by the water, while the hydrocarbon tails are shielded from it inside, the arrangement is stable — and this is why a dispersion of soap in water is stable.

The labelled diagram (see the figure) shows a **light source** sending a **beam** through two bottles placed side by side in its path. The first bottle is labelled **Solution** (a true solution) and is marked "**Light Beam not visible**"; the second is labelled **Colloidal dispersion** and is marked "**Tyndall cone; light beam is visible**".

In the true solution the path of the light cannot be detected. In the colloidal dispersion the particles scatter some of the light in all directions, so the path of the beam becomes visible as a bright cone — the **Tyndall cone** — to an observer looking at right angles to the beam. This is the Tyndall effect, and it is what distinguishes a colloidal dispersion from a true solution.

The labelled diagram (see the figure) shows a bag of **dialysing membrane** suspended in an outer trough. Inside the bag are the **dispersed phase** particles and the **dissolved electrolyte**; **water** flows in at one side of the trough and **water + electrolyte** flows out at the other.

Dialysis is the process of removing a dissolved substance from a colloidal solution by diffusion through a suitable membrane; the apparatus used is called a dialyser. A bag of a suitable membrane containing the colloidal solution is suspended in a vessel through which fresh water flows continuously. The small molecules and ions of the impurity diffuse through the membrane into the outer water and are carried away, while the large colloidal particles cannot pass through, so purified colloidal solution is left behind in the bag.

The diagram of Bredig's arc method (see the figure) is labelled: the two **metal electrodes**, the **arc** struck between their tips, the **water** (the dispersion medium) in which the electrodes are immersed, and the **ice** bath surrounding the vessel to keep the medium cool.

In this method an electric arc is struck between the electrodes of the metal immersed in the dispersion medium. The intense heat produced vaporizes the metal, and the vapour is then cooled by the surrounding medium so that it condenses to form particles of colloidal size. The process therefore involves both vaporization and condensation, and it is used to prepare colloidal sols of metals such as gold, silver and platinum.

The diagram of a soap micelle in water (see the figure) is labelled: the **hydrophilic head** (the ionic carboxylate group) of each soap molecule lying on the surface of the sphere, the **hydrophobic tail** (the long hydrocarbon chain) pointing inwards to the centre, and the surrounding \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) molecules of the dispersion medium.

In water the soap molecules arrange themselves into spherical particles called micelles. In each micelle the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails point to the centre and the hydrophilic ionic heads lie on the surface of the sphere in contact with water; as a result the dispersion of soap in water is stable.
